TaoLive Digital Avatar Agent Technical Report:
Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness

Abstract

AI-powered digital avatar streamers in live e-commerce must answer product questions, interact with viewers, and execute marketing strategies in real time, requiring low latency, frequent strategy updates, and accurate yet effective replies. To enable frequent updates, we build an evolvable Harness whose Skills, Hooks, prompts, and tools can be modified independently of model weights, allowing the system to iterate without retraining. However, not all models can benefit from Harness Evolution. Models with weak generalization—such as those trained via SFT on a single fixed Harness—overfit to the fixed configuration and cannot evolve with the Harness, while large models with strong generalization have latencies too high for real-time interaction. We propose Harness-Aware Training (HAT) to train a compact model that can evolve with the Harness. The core idea is to expose the model to diverse Harness configurations during training so that it learns to understand the current Harness rather than memorize a fixed version. HAT introduces Harness-State Augmentation (HSA), which applies task-preserving transformations to Skill identifiers, Skill content, tool schemas, prompt structure, and Hook functions, and organizes training into three stages: SFT with HSA (HSA-SFT), General Domain On-Policy Distillation (General OPD), and Agentic RL with HSA (HSA-RL). Across four complementary evaluation sets, the HAT-trained model reaches an average score of 94.8 on Live-Stream QA (base 80.3, strongest general LLM 93.0) and 94.6 on Harness-Variant QA (base 75.4). Crucially, it maintains 83.5 on IFEval, avoiding the significant 7.7-point drop typically observed after Fixed-Harness SFT. On a single NVIDIA H20 GPU (with optimization enabled), it achieves a P50 latency of 3.407 s and P95 of 8.114 s. These results demonstrate that HAT produces a compact agent that evolves with ongoing Harness changes under strict latency constraints.

TaoLive AIGC LLM Team

  

1  Introduction

Digital avatars, also referred to as virtual humans are increasingly deployed across diverse interactive applications including conversational assistants, customer service, education, and marketing (Cui and Liu, 2023; Allal-Chérif et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Among these, live-streaming e-commerce represents a uniquely demanding scenario: AI-powered digital streamers must interact with viewers in real-time, answer product questions, and execute marketing strategies under strict latency constraints (Liu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). In our application, the digital avatar’s replies are spoken publicly to the entire broadcast room, requiring the underlying agent to simultaneously satisfy three conflicting requirements. First, ultra-low latency is essential, as long wait times severely degrade the live viewing experience. Second, the agent demands high adaptability; campaign rules, compliance requirements, and reply styles change frequently driven by the shifting preferences of operations teams and merchants. Third, replies must be both accurate and effective—maintaining factual groundedness without making unsupported claims (hallucinations), while successfully addressing viewer intent.

While a standard ReAct-style loop (Yao et al., 2023) enables reasoning and tool usage, it does not facilitate agile strategy updates. In initial deployments, addressing new failure cases or modifying merchant-specific strategies often required altering central prompts or control code, followed by a full service deployment or even model retraining. This slow iteration cycle cannot keep pace with the high-frequency demands of live commerce. To address this, we propose an evolvable Harness architecture composed of four independently updatable modules: Skills (reply rules and strategies), Hooks (intermediate step validation and retry logic), a System Prompt Pipeline (dynamic instruction assembly based on context), and a Tool Registry (commerce tool definitions). This architecture allows the execution environment to evolve while policy model weights remain fixed—a practice we term Harness Evolution, which is closely related to modular prompt and runtime optimization (Khattab et al., 2023; Hebbar et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Ning et al., 2025). Our system adopts this approach through a developer-reviewed diagnose–edit–evaluate loop applied to these modules, enabling business behavior to be adjusted within hours rather than requiring a lengthy retraining cycle. (Section 2.3).

Harness Evolution, however, changes the problem that the policy model must solve. Since every promoted Harness version replaces the configuration the model was initially deployed against, the model no longer acts inside a fixed execution environment but rather inside a continuous sequence of evolving environments: Skills are rewritten, Hooks are added, prompts are reassembled, and tool schemas are renamed, all while the weights stay unchanged. Robustness to Harness changes is therefore a property the policy model must possess rather than a convenience we obtain for free; ironically, the more effective the evolution loop becomes, the more frequently the model’s environment moves beneath it.

Which model can inhabit such a moving environment? Strong zero-shot models are the natural candidates, as their general instruction-following lets them absorb a rewritten Skill or a renamed tool with no adaptation at all—but their latency rules them out, with median end-to-end latencies exceeding 11 seconds for DeepSeek-V4 models in our tests, far beyond the real-time budget. The latency requirement thus forces a compact policy model (e.g., Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), which in turn must be domain-trained, because its zero-shot accuracy does not meet industrial standards. This is where the two mechanisms collide: Fixed-Harness SFT on the single Harness configuration available at training time yields surface-form overfitting—the model memorizes specific Skill names, tool names and prompt templates instead of reading the instructions actually placed in front of it—and that configuration is precisely what Harness Evolution is designed to replace. A model trained this way becomes stale exactly when the system evolves successfully. Our experiments make this cost concrete: Fixed-Harness SFT improved domain-specific metrics but degraded general instruction-following ability (measured by IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023)) by 7.7 points, the very capability needed to follow an unfamiliar Harness. Nor do existing alternatives resolve the tension: test-time adaptation (Liang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a) violates strict latency budgets, while continual learning (Wang et al., 2024) re-pays a retraining cost for every Harness edit, which is unsustainable at our update frequency.

We resolve this tension with Harness-Aware Training (HAT), which makes the Harness state an explicit part of the training distribution rather than a fixed background assumption. Instead of fitting the policy to trajectories collected under the single configuration hth_{t} that happens to be in production, we train over a distribution of Harness states, so that the model learns to condition on whatever Harness it is currently given and can evolve together with it. Concretely, we introduce Harness-State Augmentation (HSA) to apply task-preserving perturbations to Skill content, tool schemas, prompt structure, and interaction constraints, and instantiate it in two training stages. The complete pipeline comprises (1) SFT with HSA (HSA-SFT) using trajectories generated under varied Harness configurations; (2) General On-Policy Distillation (General OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024) to recover general capabilities degraded during domain-specific SFT (Lu and Lab, 2025); and (3) Agentic RL with HSA (HSA-RL) within a production-informed live-room simulator, allowing the model to learn from the consequences of its actions under shifting environmental conditions (Zhou et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025).

Extensive evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On our real-world Live-Stream QA benchmark, the selected 35B checkpoint achieves a 94.8 average score, surpassing both the untuned base model (80.3) and strong zero-shot models. Crucially, it maintains robustness to evaluated Harness changes and avoids the significant IFEval score loss observed after Fixed-Harness SFT.

Our Harness-based judge is calibrated against human annotations to ensure reliability. In controlled deployment tests on a single NVIDIA-H20 GPU with MTP (DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Li et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2026), the complete agent meets strict latency requirements, achieving a P50 wall-clock latency of 3.407s and a P95 of 8.114s.

Our contributions are:

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    An evolvable Harness, and the training problem it creates. We decouple Skills, prompts, Hooks, and tools from the policy model, enabling agile updates to strategy and constraints without retraining; Harness Evolution alone significantly improves success rates on our development set. We then characterize its consequence: a successful evolution loop turns the policy model’s execution environment into a moving target that fixed-Harness training cannot accommodate (Section 2).

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Harness-Aware Training: putting the Harness into the training distribution. We introduce HSA and instantiate it in a three-stage HAT pipeline comprising HSA-SFT, General OPD, and HSA-RL. This design lets a latency-feasible compact model track Harness changes instead of memorizing one configuration while retaining general capabilities (Sections 3 and 5.4).

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Comprehensive benchmarks and reliable evaluation procedures. We construct four complementary evaluation sets covering real-world interactions, Harness variations, and synthetic robustness scenarios, totaling over 4,500 cases. We validate our Harness-based Agent-as-a-Judge against human labels to ensure reliable, scalable evaluation (Section 4).

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Practical insights for training agents that can evolve with their Harness. Our extensive experiments reveal critical findings, such as the larger observed impact of HSA during SFT than during RL, and the role of General OPD in recovering capabilities lost during domain adaptation (Section 5.3).

2  Digital-Avatar Harness Agent Architecture

The Harness Agent separates a slowly updated policy model from a rapidly evolving Harness state. This separation lets operators change business behavior without retraining, but it also creates the central learning problem of this paper: the policy must remain effective as the environment around it evolves. We first describe the application and runtime, then formalize the non-training process as Harness Evolution.

2.1 Live-Streaming Digital-Avatar Scenario

We study a digital-avatar host that answers product questions, handles open-ended conversation, and invokes external tools during live commerce. Public spoken responses are synthesized through TTS and avatar driving for the whole room. Each request combines the viewer message with anchor speech, product data, link IDs, and living-room status. The application demands low latency while business rules evolve weekly.

2.2 The Harness Agent Runtime

The Harness Agent runtime comprises four mechanisms. Skills are dynamically loaded behavioral modules for Q&A strategy, tool choosing, and reply style. The System Prompt Pipeline assembles instructions from product specifications, retrieved FAQ, living-room status, global boundary and active skill descriptions. Hooks validate inputs, parameters, and output formats, triggering correction or retry when needed. Tool orchestration connects the agent to external product, inventory, and commerce services. Because these modules are versioned independently of model weights, a new skill or tool can be deployed as a harness change rather than a training cycle. And our harness agent architecture is shown in Fig. 3.

2.3 Harness Evolution without Weight Updates

We use Harness Evolution to denote a controlled process that improves the agent by changing skills, prompts, hooks, or tools while holding the model fixed. It is human-in-loop rather than fully autonomous: AI performs failure clustering, diagnosis, and proposed edits; a developer confirms the plan, runs evaluation, and decides whether to promote, revise, or stop. The complete operational protocol appears in Appendix B.

Figure 2 illustrates both the value and the limit of the harness evolution process. On the 482-case human-labeled calibration set annotated by three annotators, moving from ReAct to the modular harness raises Effectiveness from 84.58 to 87.16. Evolution 1 sharply improves Accuracy from 82.40 to 92.13 but reduces Effectiveness to 84.16. Evolution 2 reaches 92.55 Accuracy and 92.75 Effectiveness. Additional long-tail rules in Evolutions 3–4 regress one or both dimensions, so Evolution 2 is selected as the engineering early-stop checkpoint. Detailed module changes, category diagnostics, stopping logic, and evidence boundaries are reported in Appendix B.

The evaluation Judge is also implemented as an editable harness agent as detailed in Appendix D.

2.4 Task and Runtime Details

This section expands the task interface and runtime inventory summarized in Section 2. Evaluation roles and scoring are specified separately in Appendix E.

Task Interface

The agent operates in live-streaming e-commerce, where a digital-avatar host responds to viewer comments under the production latency bound. Each request contains the viewer’s comment, the anchor’s nearby utterances, live-room and product context, applicable FAQ entries, and recent dialogue history. The output contains a natural-language reply—either public speech sent to TTS and avatar driving or a private text response—plus the structured tool-call trajectory used to produce it.

In single-comment mode, the runtime handles one viewer message independently; in multi-comment mode, it aggregates related messages before responding. An available internal traffic summary groups the main viewer intents as shown in Table 1. The values are rounded, and the archived summary does not preserve the reporting window; they therefore describe workload composition rather than a population estimate.

Runtime Interfaces

The Harness exposes built-in interfaces for retrieval, commerce operations, and flow control. Additional marketing interfaces are discovered dynamically from an external service through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Table 12 groups the release inventory by responsibility. The inventory is bound to manifest HA-ARL-20260614, together with the policy checkpoint and Harness version hash.

Skill Routing

Each Skill is a versioned Markdown module with YAML metadata and behavioral directives. The runtime requires at least one Reply Skill before a substantive final response; Strategy Skills are optional and can be composed when an interaction requires a specialized tool chain. Table 13 records the release inventory. Module names and versions are reconciled against the same manifest before promotion.

Execution and Trajectory Record

Figure 3 summarizes the implementation-level request path in a deliberately compact form. It separates the editable Harness modules from the repeated policy–tool loop and distinguishes resilience for an individual model call from recovery of the full trajectory. Product-specific tool names and Hook implementations are omitted because they vary across Harness versions.

A request traverses the following runtime stages:

  1. 1.

    Load and normalize context. Validate the request and assemble product, FAQ, room, and dialogue state.

  2. 2.

    Assemble the prompt. Combine the base instruction, active product and room configuration, relevant retrieved context, and any loaded Skills.

  3. 3.

    Run the agent loop. Under a configurable round limit, the policy can load Skills, issue one or more tool calls, incorporate their results, and propose a final reply.

  4. 4.

    Apply Hook checks. Lifecycle checks cover input validity, tool parameters, Skill-loading requirements, response format, known factuality risks, and retry control. The complete deployed Hook manifest remains version-bound rather than hard-coded in this description.

  5. 5.

    Extract and dispatch the reply. Remove internal reasoning fields, retain the structured trajectory, and route the public or private response to its downstream channel.

3  Harness-Aware Training (HAT)

3.1 Problem Formulation

We model a single agent interaction as πθ​(a∣x,h)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x,h), where xx denotes the user input together with its business context (e.g., live-streaming room state, current product listing), and h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} is the Harness state—the full configuration that governs agent behavior at inference time. Concretely,

h=(𝒮,𝒯,𝒫,𝒦),h=(\mathcal{S},\;\mathcal{T},\;\mathcal{P},\;\mathcal{K}), (1)

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of active Skills (pluggable policy modules with reply rules and examples), 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the tool registry (schemas, parameter definitions, and descriptions), 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the system prompt assembled by the dynamic pipeline, and 𝒦\mathcal{K} is the set of Hooks (checkpoint logic for validation, retry, and format enforcement).

In production, hh evolves continuously: operations teams add Skills weekly, tool interfaces are updated as upstream services change, and prompts are revised in response to emerging bad cases. A model trained at time tt observes hth_{t} during training but faces ht+1,ht+2,…h_{t+1},h_{t+2},\ldots after deployment.

Our training objective is twofold: (1) improve policy effectiveness when deployment draws a new harness h′∼ℰdeployh^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{E}_{\textrm{deploy}} from a specified change envelope that is broader than any single training snapshot; and (2) retain general-purpose capabilities such as instruction following after domain-specific fine-tuning.

3.2 Harness-State Augmentation (HSA)

Our working hypothesis is surface-form overfitting: when training data contains a single, fixed harness, the objective permits shortcuts such as matching skill names by string similarity, selecting tools from memorized schema text, or following instructions only in a familiar template. The core hypothesis is that changing the surface form of the harness makes it harder for the model to rely on fixed names or templates as shortcuts. If a skill is renamed, its description rewritten, and distractors injected, functional information about the skill becomes more useful for routing than memorizing a single identifier.

We perturb the harness along five dimensions, each targeting a distinct aspect of surface-form dependence:

  1. 1.

    Skill identifier We expand the skill set with synthetic plausible skills and noise skills, randomly mask subsets of existing skills, rename skills, and rewrite skill descriptions by a strong language model. These changes reduce the usefulness of a fixed skill identifier.

  2. 2.

    Skill content. Within each skill, we paraphrase individual rules, randomly mask a subset, and reorder them. This variation is intended to reduce reliance on rule position and exact wording.

  3. 3.

    Tool definitions. We rename tools, rewrite descriptions. This transformation makes name matching less reliable while preserving the tool’s function.

  4. 4.

    System prompt. We reorder top-level instruction blocks and items within blocks, and perturb numeric constraints (e.g., response length limits, maximum interaction rounds) within operationally valid ranges.

  5. 5.

    Hook. We design controlled variants of retry behavior, message structure, and hook-triggered modifications to simulate the changes that the model may encounter after hooks are updated in production.

3.3 Simulated On-Policy Environment

HSA addresses environment coverage but operates on offline demonstration data: the model learns from teacher-generated trajectories that always follow the optimal path. In real deployment, however, the agent must handle situations that never appear in demonstrations—a tool call returns an unexpected error, a Hook intercepts and forces a retry, or the agent selects a wrong Skill and must recover mid-conversation. Offline data provide no learning signal from the model’s own failed trajectories and recovery attempts, because they contain only teacher trajectories.

Moreover, the Harness Agent operates as a multi-step system: within a single user request, the model may perform Skill selection, tool invocation, result interpretation, and response generation across multiple reasoning rounds, with Hooks potentially triggering retries at each stage. Learning to navigate this dynamic interaction loop requires the model to actually experience it during training—observing the consequences of its own actions rather than imitating a teacher’s.

Environment Design

We construct a production-informed live-streaming simulator that implements the control-flow elements needed for training: skills, tool executors, hooks, and bounded multi-round interaction. The simulator consists of four components:

(1) Streaming input simulation. The environment generates realistic user inputs by sampling from a pool of live-streaming scenarios: product inquiries, casual chat, purchasing intent, after-sales questions, and mixed-intent bullet comments. Each input is contextualized with a simulated room state including current product listings, historical conversation turns, and viewer action signals (e.g., adding to cart, joining the room).

(2) Harness Agent scheduling. The simulator implements the full Harness Agent control flow. Given the model’s output at each reasoning step, the environment executes Skill routing logic (determining which Skills are loaded based on the model’s selection), triggers Hooks at the appropriate checkpoints (input validation, parameter checking, response format verification, Skill-loading enforcement), and manages the multi-round interaction loop with a configurable maximum round limit.

(3) Tool execution simulation. When the model invokes a tool, the simulator executes the call against sandboxed service replicas that return product details, pricing information, and inventory status from production catalog snapshots. The simulator also injects controlled failures—timeout errors, malformed responses, and permission denials—at calibrated rates to expose the model to error-recovery scenarios.

(4) Augmented Harness configuration. The simulated environment operates under augmented Harness states produced by the method described in §3.2. This aligns the offline and on-policy stages to the same declared change envelope.

Agentic RL Training

Within the simulated environment, we optimize the policy based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024). For each prompt, GG complete trajectory rollouts (group size) are sampled and split into tool segments and reply segments. The reward signal is computed from four dimensions:

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Accuracy: whether the final response contains factually correct information, judged during RL by a DeepSeek-V4-flash Reward Judge;

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Effectiveness: whether the response adequately addresses the user’s intent with appropriate detail and actionability;

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Tool Rationality: whether the tool invocation chain is logically sound and efficiently structured (no redundant calls, correct parameter usage);

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Skill Selection: whether the model correctly identifies the user’s intent and the current context to load the appropriate Skills.

As an auxiliary regularizer, we discourage unnecessarily long chain-of-thought (CoT) spans. For state group gg, let LigL_{i}^{g} be the sum of tokens in the CoT spans extracted from trajectory ii. Tool-call and final-reply states are measured separately, so one state does not consume the other’s length allowance. We define

rCoT​(L)\displaystyle r_{\text{CoT}}(L) ={0,L≤Llow,L−LlowLhigh−Llow,Llow<L<Lhigh,1,L≥Lhigh,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0,&L\leq L_{\mathrm{low}},\\ \dfrac{L-L_{\mathrm{low}}}{L_{\mathrm{high}}-L_{\mathrm{low}}},&L_{\mathrm{low}}<L<L_{\mathrm{high}},\\ 1,&L\geq L_{\mathrm{high}},\end{cases} (2)

Here LlowL_{\mathrm{low}} and LhighL_{\mathrm{high}} are tunable no-penalty and saturation thresholds, respectively, with Llow<LhighL_{\mathrm{low}}<L_{\mathrm{high}}; we set them to 100 and 200 tokens in the reported experiments. Thus the raw contribution ranges from 0 to −0.1-0.1 per state. This component is intended to reduce avoidable reasoning length.

The tool and reply segments are treated as separate groups (g∈𝒢={tool,reply}g\in\mathcal{G}=\{\texttt{tool},\texttt{reply}\}) for advantage computation. Since each group carries multiple reward dimensions, we adopt Group reward Decomposed Policy Optimization (GDPO) (Liu et al., 2026) to estimate advantages: for each task reward dimension dd within state group gg, a group-normalized advantage A^i(d)=(ri(d)−μg(d))/σg(d)\hat{A}^{(d)}_{i}=(r^{(d)}_{i}-\mu^{(d)}_{g})/\sigma^{(d)}_{g} is computed. The CoT score is normalized as its own dimension, A^i(CoT,g)=(q⁡(Lig)−μg(CoT))/σg(CoT)\hat{A}^{(\mathrm{CoT},g)}_{i}=(q(L_{i}^{g})-\mu_{g}^{(\mathrm{CoT})})/\sigma_{g}^{(\mathrm{CoT})}, and its negative weight is applied after this per-dimension normalization:

A^ig=∑d∈𝒟gA^i(d)−λ​A^i(CoT,g),A^ig,⋆=A^ig−μgσg.\hat{A}_{i}^{g}=\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}_{g}}\hat{A}_{i}^{(d)}-\lambda\hat{A}^{(\mathrm{CoT},g)}_{i},\qquad\hat{A}_{i}^{g,\star}=\frac{\hat{A}_{i}^{g}-\mu^{g}}{\sigma^{g}}. (3)

Here μ\mu and σ\sigma denote the corresponding within-group means and standard deviations, and all four task dimensions retain unit weight. For importance sampling, we adopt the sequence-level scheme of GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025), giving the clipped policy gradient objective:

When an individual trajectory has zero advantage after GDPO normalization, it provides no gradient signal while diluting the effective batch. Such zero-gradient samples are discarded before optimization (Yu et al., 2025). Algorithm 1 in Appendix C gives the complete procedure.

3.4 Training Pipeline

The complete training pipeline consists of three stages, each addressing a distinct capability gap:

Stage 1: SFT with Harness-State Augmentation (HSA-SFT)

HSA-SFT constructs supervised fine-tuning samples from real live-room interactions. Each original sample contains the viewer query, live-room context, and product context, and is paired with a corresponding Harness which includes the available skills, tool definitions, system prompt, and Hook configuration. To reduce the model’s dependence on the surface form of a single harness, we first apply HSA to the Harness base state in Figure 2 before generating supervised trajectories. This produces both the original Harness and multiple augmented Harness variants. HSA changes skill names and descriptions, skill-rule order, tool descriptions, system-prompt structure, and the surface form of Hook messages and retry behavior.

The teacher model then generates candidate trajectories under both the original harness and the augmented harness variants, so the supervised signals cover multiple simulated environments. These candidate trajectories are filtered according to Accuracy and Effectiveness. As a result, supervised learning exposes the student to the same task semantics under different harness realizations, encouraging it to use the functional meaning of the current Harness rather than fixed names or template matches.

Hooks in production may inform the model about formatting errors, parameter errors, or invalid outputs, and ask it to revise. We want the model to correct itself when receiving a hook reminder, but we do not want it to learn a default strategy of producing an erroneous output first and relying on retries. Therefore, for most trajectories that contain hook-triggered retries, we remove the intermediate failed outputs and hook interactions and keep only the final correct behavior. We retain a small fraction of complete retry trajectories so that the model still learns how to interpret hook reminders and recover after a failure.

Stage 2: General Domain On-Policy Distillation (General OPD)

Motivated by prior practice showing that On-Policy Distillation can improve general instruction-following ability (Lu and Lab, 2025), we add a General OPD stage after HSA-SFT. We use the pre-HSA-SFT base model as the teacher and perform on-policy distillation on the Tulu3 (Lambert et al., 2025) general instruction dataset. The student samples responses on-policy for Tulu inputs and is trained by minimizing the KL divergence between the student distribution and the base-model distribution:

ℒOPD=Ex∼𝒟gen[DKL(pθ(⋅∣x)∥pbase(⋅∣x))].\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{OPD}}=E_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\textrm{gen}}}\big[\,D_{\textrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{\textrm{base}}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\,\big]. (5)
Stage 3: Agentic RL with Harness-State Augmentation (HSA-RL)

From the checkpoint trained by HSA-SFT and General OPD, we further optimize the policy in the simulated on-policy environment. This environment uses the production-informed simulator defined in Section 3.3, including live-streaming scenarios, multi-round interaction, skill loading, tool execution, and Hooks. In HSA-RL, HSA is applied before sequence generation: before each rollout, we first decide whether the current sample uses the original Harness or an augmented Harness, and the model then generates a complete interaction trajectory under that Harness. In this way, part of the rollouts are exposed to the original production configuration, while the rest are exposed to domain-preserving augmented Harness states, maintaining adaptation to the original environment while expanding coverage of Harness changes. For optimization, we use the Agentic RL objective described in Section 3.3, with the complete training procedure provided in Appendix C.

4  Evaluation Design

This section describes the evaluation sources, the scoring metrics for each source, and the deployment replay protocol used to measure actual latency and serving performance.

4.1 Evaluation Sets and Sources

We organize the evaluation around the requirements in the live-streaming application. For offline evaluation, Live-Stream QA and Harness-Variant QA are both built from real live-room interactions and cover the main industry scenarios in our application domain, with the available internal intent mix summarized in Appendix Table 1. Live-Stream QA tests industrial reply quality, while Harness-Variant QA tests generalization and robustness to changing Harness contexts. We also use a separate real live-room calibration cohort to align the Harness-based Agent-as-a-Judge with human labels. To test broader tool and prompt robustness, we construct synthetic Tool Robustness and Prompt Robustness subsets by expanding real-industrial scenario seeds with LLM generation and consistency validation, as shown in Appendix E.3. We also evaluate general instruction-following ability on the public IFEval benchmark (Zhou et al., 2023). To test actual deployment latency and serving performance, we use a fixed complete-Agent deployment replay. Table 2 summarizes the size, source, and role of each evaluation source.

4.2 Metrics and Scoring

For Live-Stream QA and Harness-Variant QA, we evaluate each response with Accuracy and Effectiveness using the Harness-based Agent-as-a-Judge, following the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm (Zheng et al., 2024). Appendix E.1. Accuracy is a binary metric that penalizes factual errors, unsupported product claims, false promises, and capability overreach. Effectiveness measures whether the response addresses the viewer’s intent and provides useful information, with scores of 0, 0.5, or 1. We report AVG as the per-sample arithmetic mean of Accuracy and Effectiveness, computed before rounding.

For Tool Robustness and Prompt Robustness, we use task-specific rubric metrics. Tool Robustness uses ADR, RC, and TC: ADR measures whether the response addresses the core viewer query, RC measures whether the response uses the required information returned by tools, and TC measures whether the expected tool is called. Prompt Robustness uses ADR, LLM, and TCO: ADR keeps the same core-query definition, LLM evaluates whether the response satisfies the active instruction constraints, and TCO checks whether tool calls follow the required order.

For IFEval, we use its official evaluator and report prompt-level and instruction-level accuracy (abbreviated as IFE-P and IFE-I hereafter). IFE-P measures whether the model satisfies the full prompt-level instruction set, while IFE-I measures whether individual instructions are followed.

For deployment replay, we report wall-clock latency P50 and P95, TTFT, decoding throughput, execution success, and 15-second attainment. Wall-clock latency is the time from receiving the input query to obtaining the final Agent answer. TTFT is the time to the first token. Execution success indicates completion of the Agent request, not answer quality. The 15-second attainment denominator includes all measured requests.

4.3 Deployment Inference Protocol

We use 110 cases, mark 10 as warm-up, and compute metrics over the remaining 100 requests. Every request executes the complete Agent with the same Harness commit, real MCP services, at most four agent loops, and a 5-second tool timeout. Generation uses temperature 1.0 and top-pp 0.95. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and our task-trained checkpoint run in BF16 on one H20 with TP=PP=1. Their NextN MTP modules supply draft tokens, which the serving engine processes through the same EAGLE-style speculative generation and verification path with three speculative steps and four draft tokens; Appendix F.1 gives the complete engine configuration.

5  Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

The training experiments are conducted on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The training data are collected from real live-streaming scenarios, with 10K examples for SFT and 4K interaction tasks for RL. During evaluation, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and our trained checkpoints are deployed on one H20, while the Top models are accessed through Bailian API routes. We evaluate the checkpoints on the offline sets and deployment replay defined in Section 4. For 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1}–𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3}, all model comparisons use the same Harness; for 𝒯4\mathcal{T}_{4}, all models are evaluated with the same official IFEval code.

5.3 Ablation Studies

Training Pipeline Ablation

Table 4 reports cumulative training through each pathway’s shared initialization, followed by alternative Agentic RL branches under the original Harness and HSA environments.

Controlled On-Policy Optimization Comparison

We further examine the effect of OPD in our live-streaming Harness. Starting from the checkpoint before Agentic RL, we use the corresponding Agentic-RL checkpoint as the teacher and distill its behavior through OPD under the same original Harness or HSA environment.

Table 5 shows that OPD transfers part of the Agentic-RL teacher’s behavior, but its point estimates remain below the paired RL checkpoint. In the original Harness environment, OPD is lower than RL by 0.1 points on 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1}, 0.2 on IFE-P, and 4.8 on Prompt Robustness; in the HSA environment, the corresponding gaps are 0.9, 1.8, and 2.1 points.

HSA Stage Isolation

Table 6 isolates the effect of HSA at the SFT and RL stages using final checkpoint metrics from runs without General OPD. In this run, the IFE-P difference associated with HSA-SFT is +9.4, compared with +1.0 for HSA-RL, suggesting that the main HSA gain comes from the SFT stage. Figure 5 complements this table with reward-trajectory diagnostics across the four SFT/RL configurations, showing how the corresponding Accuracy, Effectiveness, Skill Selection, and Tool Rationality rewards evolve during optimization.

5.4 Controlled Deployment Inference

Table 7 reports client-observed performance in the application’s low-concurrency operating range. Every row uses the same fixed 100-case sample and complete Agent workflow; the API rows traverse vendor-managed serving routes, while all H20 rows use one local GPU.

At concurrency 1 and 2, the selected MTP configuration reaches P95 latencies of 8.114 and 9.047 s, and all measured requests satisfy the 15-second bound. On the same checkpoint and H20, MTP raises decoding throughput from 160.30 to 271.40 tokens/s at concurrency 1 (1.69×\times) and from 129.22 to 196.15 at concurrency 2 (1.52×\times). Cross-checkpoint Base–HAT Decode values are not intrinsic speed comparisons: each policy induces different Agent trajectories and completion-length distributions, and the arithmetic mean of per-call ratios is especially sensitive to very short generations. We therefore use the within-checkpoint Off–On contrast as the primary acceleration evidence. Under MTP On, HAT also has higher draft acceptance, so its remaining cross-checkpoint gap is not attributed to length alone. The offline quality values elsewhere in this section use MTP Off. A same-checkpoint, same-Judge check on 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} records 96.22 Accuracy and 94.22 Effectiveness with MTP On, compared with 95.8 and 93.8 with MTP Off; thus, no aggregate quality degradation is observed in this run. The API routes have P95 values above 21 s at concurrency 1, but their hardware, batching, and service load are not observable; we use them only as end-to-end operational references. Appendix F.1 reports the CoT-length and draft-head diagnostics, quality check, workload shape, stress-test behavior, and SGLang diagnostics.

5.5 Held-Out Evaluation of Harness Edits

We construct an additional held-out evaluation set for Harness edits by sampling 1,500 cases from real online live-streaming traffic, with 500 development cases and 1,000 held-out test cases. The raw logs contain viewer comments, dialogue history, live-room context, product information, tool-use traces, and model responses. We use an automatic quality check to count bad cases where the model output is not sufficiently natural or colloquial for a live-streaming host.

The development split is used only for Harness diagnosis and editing. We analyze the bad cases on the 500-case development set and revise editable Harness components, primarily the system prompt and Skills, while keeping the model weights fixed. The resulting Harness edits are fixed and applied unchanged to both the Fixed-Harness SFT checkpoint and the HAT checkpoint. The test split is held out from this editing loop and is used to compare each model before and after applying the same Harness edits.

Table 8 reports the held-out test results. Counts are total detected errors, so lower is better. The Harness edits reduce the total error count for both the Fixed-Harness SFT checkpoint and the HAT checkpoint, with the largest absolute reduction observed for HAT.

5.6 Human Blind-Test Protocol and Results

We conduct a human blind test to compare the modular Harness runtime with a ReAct-style baseline on real live-streaming requests. We draw a stratified 100-request blind-test set with a fixed random seed so that its scenario composition follows the full pool.

For each request, both systems run independently on the same input. The record preserves the user input, dialogue history, complete reasoning and tool-use trace, and final response from both systems. During annotation, the two responses are randomly assigned to Model A and Model B, and the annotator is not shown the system identity. The annotator chooses one of three labels: Harness better, ReAct better, or tie. Non-tie decisions require a short reason. After annotation, all 100 examples are reviewed for data consistency and labeling consistency.

Table 9 reports the preference distribution. Among the 36 examples with a clear preference, Harness wins 35, corresponding to a 97.2% non-tie win rate. A two-sided binomial test against equal preference gives p<0.001p<0.001. The only ReAct-preferred example is an ambiguous short comment, where Harness matches an irrelevant FAQ-style response while ReAct gives a safer transitional reply. We therefore treat this case as an isolated fallback-policy failure rather than a recurring disadvantage.

Table 10 summarizes the attribution of Harness wins. The largest sources of improvement are input understanding, output reliability, and scenario-appropriate behavior, which together account for 80.0% of the Harness-preferred cases. These categories include correctly separating live-room events from viewer questions, avoiding unsupported claims or false promises, handling low-information comments without forced product promotion, and using available tool evidence more appropriately. The blind-test result is consistent with the automatic Judge evaluation and provides an additional human preference check on real live-streaming requests.

5.7 Agentic Optimization Diagnostics

Figure 5 provides a diagnostic view of the four HSA configurations. The trajectories suggest that HSA-SFT primarily improves the reply-quality dimensions, while HSA-RL raises the agentic-behavior dimensions, especially Skill Selection and Tool Rationality. Overall, combining HSA-SFT and HSA-RL gives the most balanced late-stage profile across all four rewards.

6  Deployment and Production Lessons

A production live-streaming policy must simultaneously keep end-to-end P95 below 15 seconds, retain open-ended instruction following after domain training, and accommodate weekly changes to Skills, tools, and prompts. The selected HAT checkpoint meets the latency requirement in the controlled low-concurrency replay, while the reported Fixed-Harness SFT checkpoint loses general-set and prompt-robustness points. HAT and Harness Evolution are therefore operated as two independently versioned paths.

6.1 Evolution-Aware Release Process

Policy checkpoints change through HAT, whereas Skills, prompts, Hooks, and tools change through Harness Evolution (Section 2.3). A release manifest binds the policy checkpoint, Harness commit, tool schemas, fallback thresholds, and evaluation-set versions. Every proposed change runs the business regression suite and the general-capability gate before traffic promotion. Public-channel changes receive stricter review because one spoken response reaches the whole room. The non-monotonic trajectory in Figure 2 motivates an explicit early-stop rule: when long-tail fixes begin creating cross-category regressions, operators retain the last passing version rather than accumulating more rules.

6.2 Failure Containment and Recovery

The runtime uses defense in depth rather than relying on the policy alone. Parameter Hooks reject malformed tool calls before execution; tool-result Hooks convert service errors into typed observations; the Skill-loading and output-format Hooks force a bounded retry; and the loop terminates after four model rounds. A first-call timeout of 3 s, later-call timeout of 2 s, and 10 s trajectory budget trigger the compact fallback route. If recovery still fails, the system returns a conservative response or suppresses the public reply instead of inventing product facts.

Three recurrent high-severity errors shaped release checks: unsupported store or product claims, false claims that a human is driving the avatar, and tool calls that repeatedly fail or omit required parameters. Product, price, inventory, and promotion statements must be grounded in the corresponding tool result. An unsupported-claim Hook blocks unverifiable attributes, guarantees, discounts, and delivery promises; identity rules require disclosure that the host is an AI avatar. Guardrail hits, retries, fallbacks, and suppressed replies are logged with the model and Harness versions for incident review.

6.3 Low-Concurrency Serving Policy

The serving configuration uses the selected task-trained policy on one H20 with MTP enabled. The application is provisioned for one or two simultaneous requests per replica rather than high-throughput batch inference. A separate SGLang operational trace is consistent with this workload shape: sampled decode log intervals have mean 2.03 and median 1 running request, with a P95 of 7 and no queued requests in the captured window. These are log-sample-weighted scheduler observations, not a request-weighted production concurrency distribution.

The controlled replay therefore treats concurrency 1–2 as the decision-relevant range. In that range, MTP gives the selected checkpoint 1.69×\times/1.52×\times higher client-observed decoding throughput while maintaining 8.114/9.047 s P95 and 100% 15-second attainment. The concurrency 4–8 runs are stress tests: the selected checkpoint’s decoding benefit falls to 1.27×\times/1.19×\times, and MTP no longer improves P95. This boundary motivates provisioning additional replicas rather than treating MTP as a universal high-concurrency throughput optimization.

6.4 Preliminary Online A/B Test on Taobao Live

We deployed the Harness-based system in Taobao Live’s production digital-avatar business and conducted an ongoing user-level online A/B test against the existing ReAct system. Unlike the controlled replay above, this experiment measures real production traffic. Users are assigned through stable user-level bucketing. At the seven-day snapshot, the ReAct control contained 678,598 bucketed users and the Harness treatment contained 75,754, corresponding to approximately 89.96% and 10.04% of the experiment population. The arms compare complete production system versions.

We define GMV per user as multiday cumulative confirmed-receipt GMV in RMB divided by the number of bucketed users, and orders per user as completed orders divided by the same denominator. Table 11 reports only relative changes against the ReAct control because the unequal bucket sizes make raw totals unsuitable for direct comparison.

At this seven-day production snapshot, the complete Harness system shows observed preliminary uplifts of 5.54% in confirmed-receipt GMV per bucketed user and 0.80% in completed orders per bucketed user relative to ReAct. These aggregate point estimates characterize the current full-system comparison and may change as the experiment continues.

7  Related Work

Agent architectures and Harness Evolution

ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) interleaves reasoning and action in a single prompt; Toolformer (Schick et al., 2024) teaches models to invoke external tools; Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) adds within-episode self-correction. TPTU-v2 (Kong et al., 2024) improves task planning and tool use in an industrial agent system, while DSPy (Khattab et al., 2023) compiles declarative modules into optimized prompts. RIVA (Abuzakuk et al., 2026) addresses configuration-drift detection in infrastructure through cross-validating agents; our problem is complementary because the configuration being changed is the agent’s own execution environment. Harness Evolution makes that editable runtime—Skills, prompt assembly, Hooks, and tools—an explicit release process and a training-distribution object.

Prompt, schema, and agent-evaluation robustness

LLM behavior can vary under semantically equivalent prompt templates (Zhuo et al., 2024), and tool selection is sensitive to edits in natural-language tool descriptions (Faghih et al., 2025). SMART (Qian et al., 2025b) further shows that agents must learn when not to invoke a tool. These findings motivate varying prompt and tool interfaces rather than evaluating a single frozen surface form. Stateful benchmarks such as τ\tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024) and ToolSandbox (Lu et al., 2025) evaluate multi-turn interaction and intermediate state; ECom-Bench (Wang et al., 2025) adds dynamic user simulation for e-commerce customer support. Our 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} instead targets broad live-stream avatar interactions and complements the controlled Harness variants in 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2}.

Agent post-training

SFT-based agent training constructs trajectory data for instruction following and tool use (Zeng et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024); rejection-sampling and self-taught variants filter successful rollouts (Zelikman et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2023). RL methods optimize policies through environment interaction (Putta et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2024); ToolRL (Qian et al., 2025a) studies structured reward design for tool selection and application, while GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) provides the group-relative objective used here. These agent RL approaches build on the reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) paradigm (Ouyang et al., 2022) that first demonstrated effective policy optimization for instruction-following language models. RandomWorld (Sullivan et al., 2025) procedurally generates interactive tools and compositional tasks. Our environment keeps the real business ontology and randomizes the editable Harness around it. On-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024) anchors general behavior after domain SFT. Unlike work whose primary novelty is a reward, credit-assignment rule, or optimizer, our contribution lies in formulating the execution environment as a changing training-distribution object and evaluating a controlled combination of established mechanisms in production.

Training under distribution shift

Domain adaptation aligns source and target distributions (Wang et al., 2022), continual learning handles sequential tasks without forgetting (Wang et al., 2024), and test-time adaptation adjusts models at inference (Liang et al., 2024). Recent agent-specific test-time adaptation learns environment format and dynamics through deployment-time interaction (Chen et al., 2026a); it is a complementary option when changing weights or probing the environment online is acceptable. Harness-State Augmentation (HSA) is a domain-randomization instantiation (Tobin et al., 2017): it trains across controlled variation so later conditions within the declared change envelope are more likely to lie within learned support. The adaptation here is to symbolic, executable, and coupled agent configuration: a valid change may require consistent edits across Skills, prompts, tools, Hooks, and message logic. 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} evaluates in-family changes, while 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} evaluates broader in-domain scenario transfer; neither constitutes unseen-family validation.

8  Conclusion

We presented Harness-Aware Training (HAT), a systems-and-training methodology for the tension between versioned Harness change and policy stability in live-streaming digital-avatar agents. It treats Harness-state variation as a training-distribution design problem within an explicitly defined change envelope.

Our work makes four contributions. First, Harness Evolution versions runtime changes separately from policy updates through modular Skills, Hooks, prompts, and tools, and exposes the training problem created by a moving execution environment. Second, HAT treats Harness-state variation as part of the training distribution through HSA and a three-stage pipeline with HSA-SFT, General OPD, and HSA-RL. Third, scoped offline sets, a human-aligned evaluation panel, and a controlled complete-Agent deployment replay separate checkpoint quality evidence from serving-route behavior. Fourth, the ablations provide practical training insights: General OPD mainly recovers instruction-following ability after Fixed-Harness SFT, while HSA is most effective when introduced during SFT.

In our study, the HAT-trained compact model reaches 94.8 Live-Stream QA AVG and does not exhibit the general-set drop observed after Fixed-Harness SFT. On one H20 with MTP enabled, the controlled replay reaches 8.114 s P95 at concurrency 1 and 9.047 s at concurrency 2, with 100% 15-second attainment; MTP increases client-observed decoding throughput by 1.69×\times/1.52×\times over the same checkpoint without MTP. Overall, these results show that HAT can produce a latency-feasible compact agent while preserving the adaptability needed for evolving production Harnesses.

Appendix A Runtime Interface and Skill Inventories

Appendix B Harness Evolution Protocol and Diagnostics

B.1 Evolution Loop

Each Harness Evolution stage holds model fixed and changes only editable runtime modules. The evolution loop contains five steps:

  1. 1.

    AI diagnosis. Analyze the latest evaluation result, cluster the top failure causes, attach representative bad cases, and propose root causes.

  2. 2.

    Human confirmation. A developer reviews the proposed skill, prompt, hook, or tool changes, then accepts, modifies, or rejects the plan.

  3. 3.

    AI-assisted editing. Apply the confirmed changes to skill definitions, prompt assembly, Hooks, and tool logic while preserving a versioned configuration snapshot.

  4. 4.

    Human-triggered evaluation. Run inference and scoring on the dev-set.

  5. 5.

    Regression check and planning. Compare paired category changes, inspect new regressions, and let a human choose promotion, rollback, another evolution stage, or stopping.

The stopping rule is operational: stop when the remaining errors are sparse long-tail cases and local rule additions are more likely to cause cross-category regression than systematic improvement.

B.2 What Changed across Evolution Stages

The process report attributes the largest Accuracy gains to negative-feedback chat (+60.7 points), after-sales and returns (+53.3), and purchase/payment cases (+33.3). The largest Effectiveness gains occur for emotion expression (+27.3), membership or gift benefits (+18.8), and positive-feedback or already-purchased cases (+14.3). These category values are engineering diagnostics rather than pre-specified inferential analyses.

After Evolution 2, the report records 36 remaining Accuracy failures across 16 categories and 35 Effectiveness failures without a dominant systematic cluster. Evolutions 3–4 show why “more rules” is not equivalent to better evolution: targeted long-tail fixes create interactions across Skills, Hooks, and global instructions. This observation motivates configuration diversity during training and regression-aware early stopping during production evolution.

Appendix C HSA-RL Training Details

Algorithm 1 gives the complete HSA-RL training procedure that combines HSA with GDPO multi-dimensional advantage estimation, the auxiliary CoT-length dimension, GSPO sequence-level importance sampling, and zero-advantage sample filtering. Notation follows Section 3: GG is the group size; 𝒮={tool,reply}\mathcal{S}=\{\texttt{tool},\texttt{reply}\}; 𝒟tool={Tool Rationality,Skill Selection}\mathcal{D}_{\texttt{tool}}=\{\text{Tool Rationality},\text{Skill Selection}\}; 𝒟reply={Accuracy,Effectiveness}\mathcal{D}_{\texttt{reply}}=\{\text{Accuracy},\text{Effectiveness}\}; λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 is the post-normalization CoT weight; and ε\varepsilon is the PPO clip range.

Figure 6 records the corresponding single-run training diagnostics. The first-to-last 100-step window means move from 290.6 to 171.2 extracted tokens for tool-call CoT and from 93.6 to 37.0 for final-reply CoT. The logged mean penalty score q⁡(L)q(L) moves from 0.466 to 0.272, equivalent to a raw reward contribution of −0.0466-0.0466 to −0.0272-0.0272 before GDPO normalization. The strongest reduction occurs early, followed by a noisy plateau. These curves show shorter reasoning traces in this run.

Appendix D Judge as a Harness Evolution Case

The Final Evaluation Judge is a Harness-based panel that aggregates DeepSeek-V4-pro, GLM-5.2, and Qwen3.7-max by majority vote. Its Skills, prompts, and tool-verification procedures are evolved through disagreement analysis against human labels. Figure 7 shows the trajectory on 482 human-labeled interactions: Accuracy agreement moves from 81.54% at Evolution 1 to 90.46% at Evolution 6, while Effectiveness moves from a 63.70% uncalibrated baseline to an 83.40% peak. The selected multi-model voting configuration reaches 82.2% Effectiveness agreement. Disagreement clusters include missed multi-comment intents, unsupported capability claims, incorrect product linkage, and inconsistent grading of partial answers; revisions target these recurring classes rather than individual model outputs.

Appendix E Evaluation and Reproducibility Details

E.1 Judge Roles and Independence

Five roles must not be conflated: the DeepSeek-V4-pro SFT teacher generates supervised candidates; the rejection-sampling Judge filters them; the DeepSeek-V4-flash Reward Judge scores HSA-RL trajectories; the Final Evaluation Judge produces offline scores by majority vote over DeepSeek-V4-pro, GLM-5.2, and Qwen3.7-max; and human labels provide the calibration reference.

The Reward and Final Evaluation Judges have zero model overlap: DeepSeek-V4-flash is not a member of the final three-model panel. DeepSeek-V4-pro is both SFT teacher and one final voter, but a two-of-three majority prevents that vote from deciding any item alone. GLM-5.2 and Qwen3.7-max supply two non-teacher votes, and all three voters can call evidence tools when checking product facts. Human alignment is measured before the panel is used for model comparison.

E.2 Offline Scoring and Implementation

Accuracy is binary; Effectiveness uses 0, 0.5, and 1; AVG is the per-sample mean of the two computed before rounding. 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} reports Tool and Prompt robustness separately, and IFEval uses its official prompt- and instruction-level evaluators. The policy is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. HSA-RL uses GRPO with Accuracy, Effectiveness, Tool Rationality, and Skill Selection rewards under Skill, tool, prompt, Hook, and message-processing perturbations. All offline model comparisons use identical set versions and the same Final Evaluation Judge.

E.3 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} Robustness Subset Construction

𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} contains two synthetic robustness subsets generated from a real-business scenario seed library: Tool Robustness (n=1,532n=1{,}532) and Prompt Robustness (n=491n=491). The seed library is built from live-streaming e-commerce scenarios and records the product context, viewer intent, possible tool needs, and reply constraints for each scenario family.

Construction pipeline

We use a shared seed-driven generation pipeline and instantiate it into two orthogonal branches. The seed pools are extracted from real live-streaming business data, including product context, FAQ-style knowledge, dialogue history, and historical tool-use traces. For each item, an LLM generator expands a sampled business seed into a natural viewer comment, live-room or product context, and the expected behaviors to be evaluated. The generated item is then converted into the Harness input format with the corresponding tool configuration, instruction configuration, simulated tool-return map, and evaluation rubrics. We apply rule-based and LLM-based consistency checks to ensure that the query, context, tool returns, instructions, and rubrics are mutually consistent. Items that fail validation are discarded and regenerated.

The Tool Robustness subset focuses on tool selection under distractor tools, while the Prompt Robustness subset additionally constructs instruction-following prompts to test whether the model can satisfy valid prompt constraints. The corresponding metrics are Tool Called (TC), Response Contains (RC), and Addresses Core Query (ADR) for Tool Robustness, and Addresses Core Query (ADR), LLM Judge (LLM), and Tool Call Order (TCO) for Prompt Robustness. Each final item may contain multiple rubrics. AVG is the fraction of passed rubrics computed per item before aggregation. Overall, 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} tests model robustness to unseen in-domain tools and instructions in synthetic live-streaming scenarios.

E.4 Independent Bootstrap Stability Check

Table 15 reports an independent paired-bootstrap check on a separate fixed evaluation run with cached model outputs. The intervals are computed over evaluation items using 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples. Because this run regenerates model answers rather than reusing the exact outputs underlying the main tables, small differences from the main-table point estimates arise from generation stochasticity. These results are therefore used as a stability check for the qualitative contrasts rather than as replacements for the reported main results. Pboot​(Δ≤0)P_{\mathrm{boot}}(\Delta\leq 0) denotes the fraction of bootstrap replicates whose contrast is non-positive.

Appendix F Deployment Inference and Operating Details

F.1 Deployment Inference Benchmark

Protocol and Workload Shape

The deployment set contains 110 cases, with 10 warm-up cases excluded and 100 requests retained. The client runs on an office-network host Harness, real RAG and MCP services, a four-round Agent limit, and a 5-second tool timeout. Generation uses temperature 1.0, top-pp 0.95, and a 16,384-token initial generation limit with configured step-up to 65,536. The reported local configurations use one H20, BF16, TP=PP=1, and no quantization. A separate FP8 trial did not yield a material additional serving gain under this workload, so the reported runs retain BF16. The model’s NextN MTP module is the draft head; the serving engine consumes its predictions through an EAGLE-style speculative generation and verification path. Thus, NextN identifies the model-side draft module and its weights, whereas EAGLE describes how those draft predictions are used during inference.

Wall latency starts at client dispatch and ends when the Agent produces its final response. TTFT is measured to the first streamed chunk of the first model call; it includes client networking, request queueing, and server work, so it is not pure kernel prefill time. Per-call Decode TPS is completion tokens divided by call latency minus TTFT, and the table reports the arithmetic mean of these per-call ratios. This estimator is sensitive to completion length and timer granularity for very short calls; it is not an intrinsic cross-checkpoint kernel-speed measurement. We do not report client-derived Prefill TPS, TPOT, or inter-token latency, and we do not equate this per-call metric with SGLang’s interval-level aggregate generation throughput. Execution success means the Agent returned normally; it does not score response correctness. Table 18 records the workload presented to each C=1 route. Calls and tokens vary because each model chooses its own Agent trajectory. API usage supplies token counts for the remote routes; the self-hosted routes use the serving tokenizer. Token counts from different tokenizers are useful workload descriptors but are not identical measures of Chinese text length.

The output distributions explain why cross-checkpoint mean Decode TPS should be read as workload-shaped. At C=1 with MTP disabled, the Base route generates 115 tokens per call on average (median 78; P95 327.8), whereas HAT generates 106 (median 92.5; P95 230.7). Base has a 9-token call whose recorded post-TTFT interval is 1 ms, producing a 9,000-token/s ratio; consequently its mean Decode TPS is 195.42 while its median is 162.63. HAT has mean/median values of 160.30/159.71. We therefore attribute the raw Base–HAT mean gap chiefly to generated-length and trajectory distributions together with short-call timing granularity, not to intrinsic decoding speed. The within-checkpoint MTP Off–On comparisons remain the primary acceleration evidence. Under MTP On, the residual cross-checkpoint difference also coincides with the higher acceptance statistics reported in Table 20, so it is not attributed to length alone.

MTP Draft-Head Adaptation

We compare two standalone MTP-adaptation trajectories using sequences collected from HSA-RL policy rollouts. For the task-trained trajectory, the policy checkpoint starts from S0=S_{0}= HSA-SFT + General OPD, while the NextN MTP parameters are transplanted from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. For the base trajectory, the policy and its native, factory-co-trained NextN head start from the default Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint. In both cases, the policy produces rollout labels and the MTP update is performed separately: policy parameters are treated as fixed by the MTP objective, and only the draft-head parameters are optimized. Both configurations use the same EAGLE-style speculative execution path at inference, so the comparison concerns draft-weight provenance and adaptation, not different speculative algorithms.

Let a rollout be y1:Ty_{1:T} and let KK be the number of future-token offsets. The MTP loss is the standard multi-token cross-entropy that predicts token t+1+kt+1+k from the prefix through tt:

ℒMTP​(ϕ)=−1Z∑k=0K−1∑t=1T−1−klogpϕ(k)(yt+1+k∣y≤t),Z=∑k=0K−1(T−1−k),\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MTP}}(\phi)&=-\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1-k}\log p_{\phi}^{(k)}\!\left(y_{t+1+k}\mid y_{\leq t}\right),\\ Z&=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(T-1-k),\end{split} (6)

where ϕ\phi denotes the MTP parameters and k=0k=0 is next-token prediction. Thus RL supplies on-policy rollout sequences and labels, while the standalone MTP step uses only supervised multi-token CE; no reward or advantage enters Equation 6.

Despite noisy per-step losses, the grafted-head trajectory moves from a higher early-loss region toward the late-training range of the native-head trajectory. This supports the practical conclusion that a task-trained policy can accept a base-model NextN head and adapt it through subsequent standalone training on policy-rollout labels. In an unplotted pilot, omitting the base MTP initialization produced a very high initial loss. We also observed that updating the main policy while leaving the MTP head untrained reduced draft acceptance to zero, consistent with the stale draft weights no longer predicting the updated policy. These are run-specific engineering observations rather than claims of universal or multi-seed convergence.

MTP across Concurrency

Table 17 separates the deployment operating range (C=1–2) from stress conditions (C=4–8). At C=1–2, MTP increases the selected checkpoint’s Decode TPS by 1.69×\times/1.52×\times while retaining 100% 15-second attainment. At C=4–8, the speedup falls to 1.27×\times/1.19×\times and P95 no longer improves. The base model shows the same qualitative saturation boundary with a smaller low-concurrency gain. We therefore treat MTP as a low-concurrency latency optimization, not as a universal capacity multiplier.

Appendix G Deployment Workload Shape

Appendix H Supplementary Reproducibility and Deployment Details

H.1 MTP Serving Configuration

The MTP-On point estimates are not lower on either quality dimension, so this run shows no aggregate quality degradation from enabling the adapted draft head. Because sample-level paired outputs and repeated decoding runs are not available, Table 16 is not an equivalence test. Table 19 records the exact MTP serving configuration used for the reported measurements.

H.2 SGLang MTP Diagnostics

The MTP-On SGLang traces provide scheduler-level mechanism diagnostics, not request-level latency. Table 20 summarizes the captured Qwen3.6 Base window (2026-07-31 09:28–09:58) and HAT window (2026-07-30 02:35–07:23); the log timezone and platform SGLang release were not retained. The base trace’s Qwen3_5ForCausalLMMTP string is the platform’s internal implementation class for the checkpoint reported here as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

The HAT trace’s mean 2.03 and median 1 running request are consistent with the application’s low-concurrency provisioning, although the P95 of 7 shows occasional bursts. From Base to HAT, mean accept length moves from 2.94 to 3.12 and mean acceptance rate from 0.735 to 0.780; these diagnostics provide an additional mechanism-level explanation for the MTP-On cross-checkpoint TPS difference beyond output length. Acceptance measures speculative-token verification, not semantic answer quality. We omit SGLang input/gen throughput, cache occupancy, memory-usage proxies, and CUDA Graph rates because the captured windows and cache states are not aligned tightly enough for causal On/Off comparison.

H.3 Deployment Measurement Contract

Each benchmark run is bound to its run ID, policy checkpoint, Harness commit, sampled-case manifest, serving route, concurrency, generation settings, timeout rules, client region, and start/end time. H20 runs additionally record GPU count, TP/PP, dtype, MTP parameters, and known scheduler settings. Request-level records retain wall latency, first-call TTFT, every model call’s latency and usage, final execution status, and warm-up membership. A future production-traffic claim would additionally require a frozen service version, an explicit traffic window, request-weighted concurrency and queue distributions, exclusion rules, and raw telemetry.
